big_idea: Sometimes we know HOW MANY just by LOOKING — that's subitizing. Works for 1-5. Past five we count.
learning_intention: We are learning to subitize — to look at a small group of dots, paw prints, or cubes and say HOW MANY straight away, without counting one by one.
student_learning_goal: I can look at a small group and say how many without counting.
success_criteria: I can look at a flash of 1, 2, 3, 4, or 5 dots and say the number out loud before the teacher hides the card.
I can tell my partner whether the dots were in a 'dice pattern' or a 'random pattern'.
I can sort dot cards into 'easy to subitize' (1-5) and 'too many — I need to count' (6+) piles.
lesson_specific_materials: Subitizing Dot Cards (M3) — 1-5 dots, both standard dice patterns and random arrangements, plus a few 'too many' cards (6, 7, 8 dots) to seed the sort
A pile of paw-print cards (1-5 paw prints, modelled on Buddy the puppy's footprint) per partner pair
Laminated ten-frames (M2), one per partner pair
Linking cubes (5-cube sets, two colours per pair)
A small pocket chart at the carpet for whole-group flashes
A large 'subitize / count' sorting mat with two big circles labelled 'I see it!' (subitize) and 'I count it' (count)
Anchor chart paper labelled 'Subitize Without Counting — 1, 2, 3, 4, 5'

minds_on.hook: Buddy the puppy is back, and he has a NEW trick. Today he is going to show us how to spot HOW MANY paw prints he leaves WITHOUT counting them. This trick is called subitizing, and only super-fast eyes can do it.
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Hold up Buddy and a small stack of paw-print cards. 'Friends — Buddy walked through a puddle and left paw prints. I am going to FLASH a card very fast, and your job is to say how many paw prints you saw without counting one by one.'

 Hold up a 3-paw-print card. 'Watch.' Show for one second, hide it. 'How many?' Children chorus 'three'. 'Yes — and did you have time to say one … two … three? No! Your eyes JUST KNEW. That is called subitizing.' Repeat with 1, 2, 4, 5. Then flash a card with 7 paw prints — show for the same one second. Hide. 'How many?' The room will go quiet, or guesses will scatter. 'See — your eyes COULD NOT just know. Seven was too many. We have to COUNT. Today our job is to find out which numbers our eyes can JUST KNOW, and which numbers we have to count.'

Counting Crew refrain. Class chants 3x with claps: 'EYES that KNOW — to FIVE we go! That's the Counting Crew job!'
student_actions: Sit in a half-circle facing the teacher and the pocket chart.
Watch each card flash silently — no calling out before the card is hidden.
Chorus the number on the count of three after each card hides.
Notice when the room goes quiet (the 'too many' cards) versus when everyone shouts together (the 1-5 cards).

steps.instruction: Whole-group warm-up flash with the dot cards in pocket-chart. Flash 10 cards in a row, each for one second only. Mix in dice patterns (the dot pattern children know from board games) and random patterns. After every five cards, ask 'show me with your fingers' before saying the number aloud. This warms eyes and forces silent subitizing before the chorus, so you can SEE who has the answer ready and who copies the chorus.
steps.teacher_prompt: After each flash, say: 'Hold up your fingers — don't say it yet. … Now whisper to your partner. … Now say it together: THREE!' For dice-pattern cards add: 'The dots look like a dice — that helps your eyes know fast.' For random patterns add: 'The dots are scattered — but your eyes can still see TWO and ONE — that's three.'

steps.instruction: Move to partner centres in two rotations of 7 minutes each. Centre BUILD: each pair has a ten-frame, two colours of linking cubes, and a stack of dot cards. One partner flashes a card; the other partner builds the matching number on the ten-frame using cubes. Then they swap roles. Centre SORT: each pair has the big sorting mat ('I see it!' / 'I count it') and a mixed deck of dot cards (1-8 dots). They sort each card based on whether the quantity is small enough to subitize (1-5) or too many (6+). When they disagree, they hold the card up and discuss before placing.
steps.teacher_prompt: At BUILD: 'Show me on the ten-frame — if the card has 4 dots, fill 4 cells, leave 6 empty. Same number, different way of seeing it.' At SORT: 'If you had to COUNT to know, it goes in the I COUNT IT pile. If your eyes JUST KNEW, it goes in I SEE IT.'

steps.instruction: Whole class returns to the carpet for the final 4-minute 'subitize-and-tell' game. Teacher flashes one card; called-on child not only says the number but also tells HOW they saw it — e.g., 'I saw two dots and two more dots. That's four.' This narration step is critical — it is what separates 'rote-knew the answer' from 'visually decomposed the group'. Children who can narrate are securely subitizing on A6.4.
steps.teacher_prompt: After a child gives their number, ask: 'How did your eyes see it? Did you see one group, or two little groups added together?' Affirm both — children who see 4 as 'two and two' are already pre-composing for Lesson 5. Children who see 4 as 'just four' are also correct — that's the dice-pattern recognition working.

differentiation.for_emerging: Emerging children stay in the 1-3 range during the warm-up flash and the BUILD centre. The teacher adjusts their dot-card deck to remove 4-and-5 cards. At SORT, they sort only 1-5 cards (no 6+ confusers). They are assessed on subitizing 1-3 only — anything above is a stretch.
differentiation.for_extending: Extending children stretch to 6 and 7 — they are introduced to 'partial subitizing' (seeing 6 as 'two threes' or '5 and 1'). At BUILD, they predict the ten-frame layout BEFORE flipping the card ('I think 4 will be two on top, two on bottom'). At SORT, they create a third pile: 'I subitize by GROUPING' — for cards where they used a chunk strategy.
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Pre-teach 'subitize' with the gesture of rapidly opening fingers (one quick burst) versus the gesture of counting (one finger raised at a time). Use the dice patterns first — many children know dice from board games and can read 1-6 instantly even if the WORD 'subitize' is new. Provide a partner who narrates each flash aloud in the home language during the warm-up. Allow gestures-only response in the SORT centre.
differentiation.for_movement_learners: NO-PAPER, NO-PURCHASE PATH: skip the printed dot cards, paw-print cards, ten-frames, and sorting mat. Use FINGERS instead of cards — teacher flashes 1-5 fingers up for one second, children chorus the number; partner-flashes are children flashing fingers at each other. Use BODIES for ten-frames — 5 children stand in a row (top of ten-frame), 5 in a row below (bottom); 'fill' the frame by having children sit/stand based on the number called. Whole lesson runs on hands, fingers, and bodies — no purchased cards, no laminated frames, no sorting mat.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: (a) on the warm-up flash, does the child have the answer ready BEFORE the chorus (seen by finger-up speed), or do they wait and copy peers? (b) at BUILD, does the child place the right number of cubes on the FIRST attempt, or do they re-count and adjust? (c) at the subitize-and-tell narration, can the child tell HOW their eyes saw the number ('I saw three and one — that's four'), or do they just say the number without explanation? Children who narrate AND build correctly on the first try are securely subitizing on A6.4.
formative_check.how_to_record: Per-child tally sheet: out of 5 quick flashes (1, 2, 3, 4, 5 dots, in random order), how many did the child get right BEFORE the chorus prompt. A score of 4-5 = secure A6.4. A score of 2-3 = developing. A score of 0-1 = needs revisit. Plus a comments column for children who use a 'two-and-two' chunk strategy (an early-composing signal worth flagging for Lesson 5).

consolidation.activity_name: Counting Crew Conversation — Eyes That Know
discussion_prompts: Buddy wants to know — what is the BIGGEST number our eyes can just KNOW without counting? (Answer: five.)
Mae just asked us — when she sees a dice and rolls a 4, does she count the dots or just KNOW? Why?
Show me with your hands: ONE big group of 6 versus TWO little groups of 3 — which is easier to subitize? Why?
consolidation.exit_routine: Refrain chant 3x. s the Counting Crew job!' Then on the way out, the teacher flashes ONE final card per child (1-5 dots). Each child whispers the number into the teacher's ear. Teacher tallies: green sticker for instant correct, yellow for hesitated-then-correct, red for needed counting. The class wall has a 'Subitize Wall of Fame' chart that fills with green stickers as the unit progresses.

assessment_in_this_lesson.evidence_collected: Per-child subitize-out-of-5 score from the warm-up flash. Photo of each pair's BUILD ten-frames showing a sequence of correctly built quantities. Photo of each pair's SORT mat showing 1-5 in 'I see it' and 6-8 in 'I count it'. Exit-routine sticker tally (green/yellow/red) feeding the 'Subitize Wall of Fame' chart. A short audio note (teacher voice memo) of two or three children's narration during subitize-and-tell, capturing the 'two and two makes four' chunk-strategy signal.
assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: A6.4 'subitize quantities to 5' is THE central skill of K number sense — children who can subitize 1-5 enter Grade 1 with strong perceptual number anchors. The formative tier here feeds directly into Lesson 5 (composing/decomposing), which is built on subitizing — children who can see 4 as 'two and two' have already begun composing. The flash-and-narrate format gives a tight, observable window into A6.4 progress and is repeatable as a 60-second check on any later day to track growth across the unit.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the Child Counts Instead of Subitizing — re-tuning the eye to the dice pattern (Clements, 1999; Sarama & Clements, 2009; Kaufman et al., 1949; Baroody, 2006)
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
On A6.4 subitizing to 5, the central K trap is the child who CAN see a 4-dot card and CAN say 'four' — but only after touching each dot one by one with their finger and counting subvocally. Counting-then-saying is NOT subitizing.

Kaufman et al. (1949) established the original perceptual subitizing limit at 1-4 — the maximum quantity human eyes recognise without serial counting. Above 4, performance shifts from instant recognition to either grouping (chunked subitizing) or counting. K children are at the cusp of this transition; the lesson's flash protocol is engineered to find each child's edge.

Clements (1999) — in 'Subitizing — what is it? Why teach it?' — distinguishes PERCEPTUAL subitizing (instant recognition of 1-3 or 1-4 in any arrangement) from CONCEPTUAL subitizing (using known patterns or chunks to recognise larger quantities — seeing 5 as 'a dice-5 pattern' or seeing 6 as 'two threes'). Both are counted as subitizing under A6.4 — what matters is that the child arrives at the answer WITHOUT serial counting.

Sarama & Clements (2009) place perceptual subitizing as a precursor in the K trajectory: it is the foundation on which conceptual subitizing, then composing/decomposing (Lesson 5), then mental addition is built. Children who exit K still finger-counting will struggle with all derived facts in Grade 1 because they have no perceptual anchor for small quantities.

Baroody (2006) traces the development of single-digit recognition through three phases: counts every time, dice-pattern recognition, full conceptual subitizing including random arrangements. The 'random patterns can't be subitized' misconception below maps onto the dice-only phase — children stuck there need explicit chunk teaching ('two and one is three') to progress.

Why this matters: a K child who exits with no subitizing will count from 1 every time they need a small quantity for the next two years. The repair is two-fold: (a) reduce the flash time so finger-counting is impossible, and (b) give the child the dice-pattern shortcut so their eye has a CHUNK to grab onto.

This walkthrough covers a pair's BUILD centre when one child was finger-counting on the warm-up.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Warm-up flash has just ended. You're moving children to the BUILD centre. One specific child (call her Alex) got 5/5 on the warm-up flash — but you watched her finger-tap each dot card with her index finger before answering. Her answers were correct, but they were SLOW (~3-4 seconds each) and visually mediated by counting. Now Alex is at BUILD with her partner. You stop by their station 90 seconds in.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script: Crouch beside Alex. Pick up a dice-pattern 4-card (the standard dice-4 layout with dots at the four corners). Don't flash it — show it openly. 'Alex, look at this card. Don't tell me the number. Look at the SHAPE.' Pause. 'How many corners does this dot-pattern have?' She'll say 'four' (corners is a known word). 'Yes — and the dots are at every corner. So this is the dice-4 pattern. Anytime you see this shape — boom — your eyes know it is four. You don't have to count.' Now flip the card face down. Flip it back up for one second. Hide it. 'How many?' She says 'four'. 'Did you count?' She'll think — usually says no. 'GREAT — your eyes JUST KNEW because you remembered the shape.' Repeat with the dice-3 pattern (a diagonal of 3 dots). 'This is the dice-3 — a slanted line. Three dots on a slant.' Flash, hide. 'How many?' Then dice-2 (two dots opposite corners). Then dice-5 (four corners + a centre dot). Don't do dice-1 (it's trivial). After all four, mix the deck and re-flash quickly — 0.7 to 1.0 second per card. Watch her finger. If it stays still, she is now subitizing. Tick the 'subitize_score' column with a note: 'switched from count-on-fingers to instant — used dice patterns'. If her finger STILL twitches toward the card, drop to a 0.5-second flash for two more rounds. Past that, she is genuinely on the subitize-by-counting boundary and needs the random-pattern recovery from the next planning cycle.
expected_student_responses: (Confused) Finger-taps each dot during the warm-up flash, gives correct answers slowly. The card might as well not have been hidden.
(Mid) After the dice-pattern teach-in, can subitize dice-3, dice-4, dice-5 instantly but slips back into counting on random patterns. Normal — random subitizing develops after dice subitizing.
(Strong) Recognises dice-4 as four AND when shown a random-4 (e.g., a Y-shape of dots) says 'four — three plus one'. Has internalised both pattern-based AND chunk-based subitizing.
(Stretched) Volunteers without prompting: 'I bet 6 is just two threes' or 'a dice-5 plus one is six'. Generalising the chunk strategy beyond five — flag for Lesson 5 stretch.
common_misconceptions: Subitizing means counting fast. (Child believes the only difference between subitizing and counting is speed. The repair is to make the flash so fast that finger-counting is impossible — then the child realises their EYES did the work, not their finger.)

Random patterns can't be subitized. (Some children can subitize dice patterns but freeze on random arrangements. The repair is the chunk strategy: 'I see two and one — that's three.' Random subitizing is composed, not perceptual, but counts as A6.4.)

Past five is impossible. (Children correctly observe their eyes can't subitize 7 — but some over-generalise to 'past five there is no shortcut'. In Lesson 5 they will learn the 'I see 5 and 2 more' decomposition. Don't worry about this misconception today; it self-resolves.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child finger-counts every flash (still on Baroody 2006 phase 1 'counts every time'): drop the flash time. If the child finger-counts, they are getting too much exposure. Reduce from 1 second to 0.7 to 0.5 — past that, the eye HAS to do the work. Pair shorter flashes with the chorus 'EYES that KNOW — to FIVE we go!' so anti-counting is the rule, not finger-tapping.

DIAGNOSTIC B — child subitizes dice patterns instantly but freezes on random arrangements (Clements 1999 perceptual-only, no conceptual subitizing yet — overgeneralised dice dependency): teach the dice-pattern shortcut, then explicitly bridge to chunks: hold a random-4 (Y-shape) and say 'three on top, one below — three and one is four'. Make the chunk verbal AND visual; have child ECHO the chunk. Repeat with random-3 (one + two), random-5 (three + two). Conceptual subitizing is composed, not perceptual, but counts as A6.4.

DIAGNOSTIC C — child overgeneralises 'two' (says 'two' for any small group of 1, 2, or 3 dots — perceptual subitizing not yet differentiating within the 1-4 range, Kaufman 1949 cusp): drop to 1-2-3 only; flash dice-1, dice-2, dice-3 in alternating order; force differentiation. Have child BUILD the pattern themselves on the ten-frame after each flash — placing the cubes physically teaches the difference between two cubes and three cubes that the eye has not yet differentiated.

worksheet_brief.worksheet_title: Subitize: How Many at a Glance
worksheet_brief.purpose: End-of-lesson consolidation. Children practise subitizing 1-5 on paper using printed dot cards and tally what they 'just saw' versus what they had to count. Captures formative-level evidence for A6.4 — every child produces a written record of which quantities they subitize fluently. Goes home as a take-home practice sheet ('Show your family how fast your eyes can spot a number').

parts_outline.task: Look at each dot card for a moment. Write the number you saw without counting. (Five cards, dice patterns 1-5.)
Some cards are easy to subitize, some are not. Cut out the cards and sort them: 'I see it!' (1-5 dots) and 'I count it' (6 or more dots).
Buddy left some paw prints. Circle the groups your eyes can JUST KNOW (subitize). Cross out the groups you have to count.
